Yes. Nuclear warheads are made of one or more masses of fissile, radioactive material which are caused to be above a certain threshold of mass & density which (very likely) causes a chain reaction of atoms splitting apart.

Now for material to be radioactive, it needs some of its constituent atoms to emit particles via a process known as decay. These particles have mass, which causes the emitting atoms to lose the same amount of mass. This decay is a loss of subatomic (or atomic) particles, and it happens due to an atom's inherent instability.

Over time, these atoms lose enough of their particles to no longer be the same particle it once was. it may be a different, less massive isotope or it may be a different less massive element altogether (depending on the kind of decay). The more radioactive a substance, the faster the decay. The average amount time it takes for this decay to occur in a substance is known as the substance's half-life.

In the case of nuclear warheads, being highly radioactive, they decay relatively quickly. Only a small amount of the nuclear material needs to undergo this process to significantly reduce the odds of a fission chain-reaction occurring.
